title: Water and Your Body
summary: Why more than half of your body is water, the jobs water does inside you, how you lose it, and how to drink enough, especially in a hot Saudi summer.
poll: You only need to drink water when you feel thirsty.

versions.title: You Need Water
versions.text:
Your body is more than half water. It is in your blood and bones. You need it to live.

Blood is mostly water. It flows all through you. It brings food to each part. It brings air, too.

On a hot day, you sweat. The sweat dries on your skin. That cools you down.

Your kidneys help, too. They clean your blood. They take out waste. The waste leaves as urine.

Water makes spit in your mouth. Spit helps you eat. Water pads your joints. It keeps your brain safe.

You lose water all day. It goes out in sweat and urine. It goes out when you breathe, too.

Need water? You feel thirsty. Then drink! Too little can make your head hurt. It can make you tired. Look at your urine. Dark yellow means drink more. Light is good.

You can live for weeks with no food. But you can live just a few days with no water!

Drinks give you water. So does food. A melon is full of water.

Saudi summers are hot. It can top 45 degrees! So sip it all day. Play sports? Drink more. Pick water, not sweet drinks.

On a hot day, or when you run, you sweat. The sweat dries on your skin. As it dries, it cools you down.

You lose water all day long. It goes out in sweat and urine. Some even goes out each time you breathe.

A person can live for weeks with no food. But we can live for only a few days with no water!

Drinks give you water, and so do foods. A melon is mostly water.

Saudi summers are very hot. It can be more than 45 degrees! So sip water all day. Drink more when you play sports. Pick water, not sweet drinks.

versions.title: Water and Your Body
versions.text:
Did you know that your body is more than half water? There is water in your blood, your skin, your muscles, and even your bones. You could not live without it.

Your blood is mostly water. It flows through your whole body. As it moves, it carries food and oxygen to every part of you.

On a hot day, or when you run and play, you sweat. The sweat sits on your skin and dries. As it dries, it takes heat away and cools you down.

Your kidneys need water, too. They clean your blood and take out waste. The waste leaves your body as urine.

Water makes the spit in your mouth. Spit helps you chew and swallow your food. Water also pads your joints, such as your knees. It helps keep your brain safe, too.

You lose water all day long. It leaves in sweat and urine. Some even leaves each time you breathe out.

When your body needs more water, you feel thirsty. Try not to wait too long. Too little water can give you a headache and make you feel tired. You can check the color of your urine. Dark yellow means you should drink more. Pale yellow means you are fine.

A person can live for weeks without food. But we can live only a few days without water!

You get water from drinks, and also from food. A watermelon is mostly water.

Summers in Saudi Arabia are very hot. It can be more than 45 degrees! So sip water all through the day, and drink more when you play sports. Choose water instead of sweet drinks.

versions.title: Water and Your Body
versions.text:
Did you know that more than half of your body is water? There is water in your blood, your skin, your muscles, and even your bones. Without it, you could not stay alive.

Your blood is mostly water. It flows through your whole body, carrying food and oxygen to every part of you. Without enough water, your blood could not do this job well.

On a hot day, or when you run and play, you sweat. The sweat sits on your skin and slowly dries. As it dries, it carries heat away from your body and cools you down.

Your kidneys need water, too. They clean your blood and remove waste. The waste then leaves your body as urine.

Water also makes the spit in your mouth, which helps you chew and swallow food. In addition, water pads your joints, such as your knees and elbows. It even helps protect your brain.

Every day, you lose water. It leaves your body in sweat and urine. Some even leaves each time you breathe out.

When your body needs more water, you feel thirsty. It is best not to wait too long. Too little water can give you a headache and make you feel tired. One easy check is the color of your urine. Dark yellow means you should drink more, while pale yellow means you are fine.

Amazingly, a person can live for weeks without food. But we can survive only a few days without water!

You get water from drinks, and also from foods. A watermelon is mostly water.

In Saudi Arabia, summers are very hot. Temperatures can rise above 45 degrees! So sip water all through the day, and drink extra when you play sports. Water is a better choice than sweet drinks.

versions.text:

Your blood is mostly water, and as it continues to circulate through your entire body, it transports nutrients from your digested food and oxygen from your lungs to every living cell. Without sufficient water, your blood could not perform this essential task properly.

Water also helps your body regulate its temperature. On a hot day, or whenever you exercise, you sweat, and the sweat remains on your skin until it begins to evaporate, which means it gradually changes into a gas, and as it evaporates, it carries heat away from your body, cooling you down.

Your kidneys also depend on water, because they filter your blood and remove waste, which then leaves your body as urine.

Water also produces saliva, the liquid in your mouth that helps you chew and swallow food. Additionally, water helps to cushion your joints, such as your knees and elbows, and it surrounds and protects your brain.

Every single day you lose water, which leaves your body in sweat and urine, and a small amount even escapes in your breath each time you exhale.

When your body requires more water, you feel thirsty, and it is wise not to ignore this signal. If you do not drink enough, you can become dehydrated, and you may develop a headache or feel unusually tired. One simple test is the color of your urine: dark yellow indicates that you should drink more, while pale yellow suggests that you are well hydrated.

Remarkably, a person can survive for weeks without food, but only a few days without water.

You obtain water from beverages and also from foods such as watermelon and cucumber, which consist mostly of water.

In Saudi Arabia, summers are extremely hot, and temperatures can climb above 45 degrees Celsius, so you should sip water throughout the day and drink extra when you play sports. Water is a healthier choice than sugary drinks, which contain unnecessary sugar.

versions.title: Why Your Body Depends on Water
versions.text:
It is a striking physiological fact that water constitutes roughly 60 percent of an adult's total body mass, permeating the blood, the skin, the musculature, and even the rigid architecture of the skeleton; consequently, without a consistent and adequate intake, survival for any extended period becomes impossible.

Blood itself is composed predominantly of water, and as this fluid circulates ceaselessly through an intricate network of vessels spanning the entire body, it delivers nutrients extracted from digested food and oxygen absorbed within the lungs to each of the body's countless living cells, a transport function that would be rendered impossible without sufficient hydration.

Water additionally enables the body to regulate its internal temperature with remarkable precision. During intense heat or vigorous physical exertion, perspiration accumulates on the skin until it evaporates, a transformation from liquid to vapor that carries thermal energy away from the body and thereby produces a cooling effect.

The kidneys, too, depend entirely on water, since they perform the continuous task of filtering the bloodstream, extracting metabolic waste products that are subsequently excreted as urine. Water further contributes to the production of saliva, the fluid that facilitates chewing and swallowing, and it serves to cushion the joints, including the knees and elbows, while simultaneously surrounding and safeguarding the delicate tissue of the brain.

Water is lost continuously, through perspiration, urine, and even the imperceptible vapor exhaled with every breath, and the body signals this depletion through the sensation of thirst, an instinct that should never be disregarded. Neglecting this signal can precipitate dehydration, often manifesting as headaches, exhaustion, or irritability. A simple and effective diagnostic method involves observing urine color: a dark yellow hue indicates insufficient hydration, whereas pale yellow suggests the body is adequately hydrated.

It is a remarkable testament to water's biological necessity that while a person may survive several weeks without food, deprivation of water typically proves fatal within only a few days. Fortunately, hydration is obtained not merely through beverages but also through water-rich foods such as watermelon and cucumber, whose cellular structure consists largely of water.

In Saudi Arabia, where summer temperatures regularly exceed 45 degrees Celsius, maintaining consistent hydration throughout the day is essential, and additional water should be consumed during athletic activity, when perspiration losses accelerate considerably. Plain water remains the preferable choice over sugary beverages, which supply superfluous calories without any corresponding hydrational or nutritional benefit. Maintaining this delicate fluid balance, therefore, is not a minor lifestyle preference but a continuous physiological necessity that underlies virtually every function the body performs.

versions.title: Why Your Body Depends on Water
versions.text:
Approximately 60 percent of adult body mass consists of water, a substance so thoroughly integrated into human physiology that it permeates the bloodstream, the dermal and muscular tissues, and even the ostensibly solid architecture of the skeletal system; its chronic insufficiency, therefore, precipitates physiological failure within a remarkably short interval.

Blood, itself predominantly aqueous in composition, circulates continuously through an elaborate vascular network that extends to every anatomical region, transporting nutrients derived from digestion alongside oxygen absorbed within the pulmonary tissue to the innumerable cells that constitute living tissue; this essential transport mechanism would be rendered entirely nonfunctional in the absence of adequate hydration.

Thermoregulation constitutes another indispensable function water performs within the body. Under conditions of elevated ambient temperature or vigorous physical exertion, the sweat glands secrete perspiration onto the cutaneous surface, where it subsequently undergoes evaporation, a phase transition from liquid to vapor that extracts thermal energy from the body and thereby regulates internal temperature with considerable efficiency.

The renal system, comprising the kidneys, depends entirely upon a sufficient aqueous supply, since these organs perform the continuous physiological task of filtering circulating blood and extracting metabolic waste products, which are subsequently expelled as urine. Water additionally facilitates the synthesis of saliva, the digestive fluid essential to mastication and deglutition, while simultaneously providing a cushioning function for the articular joints, including the knees and elbows, and enveloping the cerebral tissue within a protective aqueous barrier.

Water depletion occurs continuously and through multiple physiological pathways: perspiration, urinary excretion, and the imperceptible vapor exhaled with each respiratory cycle. The body signals this progressive depletion through the sensation of thirst, a biological imperative that should never be disregarded, since its neglect can precipitate dehydration, frequently manifesting through cephalic pain, lethargy, or irritability. A straightforward diagnostic indicator involves observing urinary coloration: a notably dark yellow hue suggests inadequate hydration, whereas a pale yellow tone indicates the body has maintained sufficient fluid balance.

It constitutes a remarkable testament to water's physiological indispensability that although the human body can endure several weeks of complete food deprivation, the absence of water typically proves fatal within a matter of days, a stark asymmetry that underscores water's biological primacy over nutrition itself. Hydration, fortunately, derives not exclusively from direct consumption of beverages but also from water-dense foods such as watermelon and cucumber, whose cellular composition consists overwhelmingly of water.

Within Saudi Arabia, where summer temperatures routinely surpass 45 degrees Celsius, consistent hydration throughout the diurnal cycle becomes a physiological necessity rather than a mere recommendation, and supplementary water intake is particularly crucial during athletic exertion, when perspiration-induced fluid loss accelerates substantially. Plain water remains categorically preferable to sugar-laden beverages, which contribute superfluous caloric content while offering no commensurate hydrational or nutritional advantage, and which may, over time, contribute to broader metabolic imbalances.

questions.stem: What is this article mostly about?
options: Why sweet drinks are bad for you
Why kidneys are the most important body part
Why your body needs water to work well
Why summers in Saudi Arabia are hot
questions.why: The whole article tells the jobs water does in your body and how to get enough of it.

wrong.A: Sweet drinks are named only at the end.
wrong.B: Kidneys are one part of the article, not the main idea.
wrong.D: Hot summers are one reason to drink, not what the whole article is about.

questions.stem: What does sweat do as it dries on your skin?
options: It cools you down.
It cleans your blood.
It makes spit.
It feeds your bones.
questions.why: The article says sweat dries on your skin, and that cools you down.

wrong.B: The kidneys clean your blood, not sweat.
wrong.C: Water makes spit in your mouth, but sweat does not.
wrong.D: The article does not say sweat feeds bones.

questions.stem: What do your kidneys do?
options: They make the sweat on your skin.
They pad your knees and elbows.
They bring air to each body part.
They clean your blood.
questions.why: The article says the kidneys clean your blood and take out waste, which leaves as urine.

wrong.A: Sweat comes out of your skin. The article does not say kidneys make it.
wrong.B: Water pads your joints, not the kidneys.
wrong.C: Blood brings air and food to each part.

questions.stem: What does the word thirsty mean in this article?
options: Very hot
Needing a drink
Very sleepy
Feeling full
questions.why: The article says you feel thirsty when your body needs water, and then you should drink.

wrong.A: Being hot can make you thirsty, but the word does not mean hot.
wrong.C: Feeling tired is a sign of too little water, not the meaning of thirsty.
wrong.D: Thirsty means you want a drink, not that you are full.

questions.stem: Ali played football on a hot day. Now his urine is dark yellow. What should he do?
options: Eat a big meal
Go to sleep
Drink some water
Run some more
questions.why: The article says dark yellow urine means you should drink more water.

wrong.A: The article links dark yellow urine to water, not food.
wrong.B: Sleep will not give him the water he needs.
wrong.D: Running more would make him sweat and lose even more water.

questions.stem: What can happen if you have too little water?
options: Your head may hurt.
Your bones will grow faster than before.
You will want to eat much more food.
Your skin will turn a yellow color.
questions.why: The article says too little water can make your head hurt and make you tired.

wrong.B: The article does not connect water with fast-growing bones.
wrong.C: The article does not say you will get hungry.
wrong.D: The article talks about yellow urine, not yellow skin.

questions.stem: Why does the article say to drink more when you play sports?
options: Sports make your kidneys stop working.
You cannot breathe well while you play.
Water helps your legs run much faster.
You sweat more and lose water.
questions.why: When you play, you sweat, and sweat is one way you lose water. So you need to drink more to put it back.

wrong.A: The article never says kidneys stop.
wrong.B: You breathe all the time, even while you play.
wrong.C: The article does not say water makes you faster.

questions.stem: Why does the author tell us that people can live for weeks with no food but only a few days with no water?
options: To show that food is not good for you
To show how much we need water
To tell how to make a meal
To teach how to grow food
questions.why: This fact shows that water is even more important to stay alive than food.

wrong.A: The author does not say food is bad. We need both.
wrong.C: The article does not tell how to make a meal.
wrong.D: The article is not about growing food.

MID.prompt: Imagine you are planning a school sports day in June. Using facts from the article, explain what you would do to keep everyone from becoming dehydrated.
checklist: I gave at least two clear steps.
I explained each step with a fact from the article.
I used the words dehydrated and evaporate correctly.
MID.modelAnswer: For a June sports day, I would tell everyone to drink water throughout the day, not just when they feel thirsty, because sweat evaporates off your skin to cool you down and that lost water needs to be replaced. I would also plan extra water breaks during hot games, since playing hard makes you lose even more water and can leave you dehydrated with a headache or a tired feeling. Bringing watermelon as a snack would help too, since foods with lots of water can also keep everyone from becoming dehydrated.

keyWords.definition: to move around through a system and come back to the start

keyWords.definition: to control something and keep it at the right level

keyWords.definition: to clean something by passing it through a part that catches what is not wanted
keyWords.example: The machine will filter the water before we drink it.

keyWords.definition: to protect something by softening a hit or rubbing
keyWords.example: Thick socks cushion your feet when you run.

keyWords.definition: having enough water in your body
keyWords.example: Athletes stay hydrated by drinking small amounts of water often.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the article?

HIGH.prompt: The poll says you only need to drink water when you feel thirsty. Do you agree or disagree? Use at least two facts from the article to support your answer.
checklist: I clearly stated whether I agree or disagree.
I supported my opinion with at least two accurate facts from the article.
I used the words regulate and hydrated correctly.
HIGH.modelAnswer: I disagree that you only need to drink water when you feel thirsty. Thirst is already a sign your body needs more water, so waiting for it means you may already be a little dehydrated and could develop a headache or feel tired. Water also helps your kidneys filter waste out of the blood that circulates through your body, and it helps regulate your temperature as sweat evaporates, so drinking steadily throughout the day, especially in Saudi Arabia's extreme summer heat, keeps you better hydrated than waiting until you are thirsty.
